subject: computer-science

items.q: What is the worst-case complexity of bubble sort?
items.misconception: O(n) because it just passes through the list.
items.why: Students count one pass and forget that bubble sort does up to n passes, each comparing up to n elements. The nested loop structure gives n times n = n squared.

items.q: Which search is fastest on a large sorted list?
items.why: The answer examiners want is: Binary. “Linear” is the distractor this question was built around — if it tempted you, that's the exact gap to close.

items.q: Which sort works by inserting each item into a sorted prefix?
items.why: It's Insertion sort. “Bubble sort” is the classic near-miss here; knowing why it's wrong is worth as much as knowing the right answer.

items.q: In the best case, how many comparisons does linear search make if the target is first?
items.why: The real figure is 1. The wrong options cluster deliberately close — anchor the exact number to one concrete fact so it can't drift.
